newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy says "Ciao Marcello," thanks for sweet life.
newsitem.headline: Italy says "Ciao Marcello," thanks for sweet life.

text.p: A mournful Italy heaped praise on Marcello Mastroianni on Friday as it prepared to bury the actor who symbolised both the suave Latin Lover and the ordinary next door neighbour to two generations.
"Farewell Marcello, you made our life sweeter," Milan's Corriere della Sera said in a headline reflecting the sorrow of Italians who felt they lost a friend rather than a star.
Italian media gave blanket cover to the death of Mastroianni in Paris on Thursday at the age of 72. One national newspaper dedicated its first nine pages to his career.
Perhaps the most powerful and poignant tribute was sketched in a small cartoon on the front page of Rome's La Repubblica.
It showed the late director Federico Fellini, who died in 1993, standing on a cloud beckoning Marcello to heaven. "Marcello, come. It's wonderful," Fellini says in English.
Those were the exact words that blonde siren Anita Ekberg used to coax the reluctant Mastroianni to wade with her in the Trevi Fountain in "La Dolce Vita" (The Sweet Life), which Fellini directed.
That black-and-white scene remains one of the most memorable in the history of cinema, etching Mastroianni's boyish, handsome face in the minds of millions.
Within hours of his death television stations ran his most famous films, including "Yesterday, Today and Tomorrow," "Marriage Italian Style," and "A Special Day".
"The sweet life of a man on the run," was the headline chosen for a comment by Enzo Biagi, one of the few journalists in whom Mastroianni confided.
Mastroanni never liked the label of Latin Lover that his early films glued on him for life. Friends say he was a down-to-earth man who enjoyed life's simple pleasures most.

"After a hard, tense day of filming, he always knew how to help everybody let off steam," said a stagehand at Rome's Cinecitta studios. "He would say: 'Ok, forget about what we said to each other today, where are we all going to eat?'".
Everyday Romans knew he really never stopped being one of them, popping up at the same restaurants, driving his own car.
That sentiment was clear on a banner hung on the rails of the Trevi Fountain during the night. It read "Roma per Marcello (Rome for Marcello).
A large picture of Mastroianni in his later years with actor Massimo Troisi, also dead, was placed in front of the fountain, where Romans dropped flowers.
A nun standing in a moment of reflection at the Trevi on Friday morning said: "He was a great personality. He believed in something. He left a memory for all of us."
Her sentiment was a far cry from the Roman Catholic Church's stand on Mastroianni in 1960 when the Vatican condemned La Dolce Vita as the work of the devil.
Sophia Loren, who with Mastroianni formed perhaps cinema's most famous screen couple since Spencer Tracy and Katherine Hepburn, said she felt like part of her had died.
"This is the most pain I have felt since the death of my mother," she said.

"I am really very, very sad because he was genuinely a sweet man," said Jack Lemmon, who starred with Mastroianni in "Maccheroni," in which Marcello played a Naples bank employee who wrote plays on the side.
Mastroianni's body was being returned to Rome on Saturday morning. He will lie in state at city hall until Sunday's funeral there and be buried in the family tomb at the Verrano cemetery.
